newsitem.title: UK: TIGHT ZINC MARKET MULLS WHETHER LME TO INTERVENE.
newsitem.headline: TIGHT ZINC MARKET MULLS WHETHER LME TO INTERVENE.

text.p: Zinc premiums for cash over three months metal are approaching historic highs, but the London Metal Exchange (LME) is unlikely to intervene unless the nearby spreads flare, traders and analysts said.
Any action by the LME would wait until the run-up to the September delivery date, where most of the tightness is centred, they added.
The premium of cash over metal for delivery in three months flipped out to $175 per tonne on Monday, close to highs of $190 in 1992 and $230 in 1989. It eased to about $145 on Tuesday.
The LME intervened in both 1992 and 1989, but only to limit the daily premiums.
"As long as the nearbys -- the cash-for-a-day, cash-for-a-week -- are in a contango, they will probably take no action," said one European trader.
The nearby spreads are in contango until the September delivery date in the third week of next month.
The scramble for metal stems from a move by Chinese smelters last year to sell forward huge amounts of metal at around $1,100 per tonne.
The premium for September delivery has shot up as a European merchant and investment funds keep a tight grip on the metal for the important dates, analysts said.
The premium for the September delivery date over metal for one week later was $55 on Monday.

The LME seeks to allow market forces to operate unless a "disorderly" market is threatened. When market players are unable to cover positions just before the delivery date, intervention is seen as necessary.
Analysts say Chief Executive David King would analyse data from the LME's large position reporting data and see if those positions move in tandem with the tightening of the nearby spreads.
Some of the long positions held by funds are equivalent to double the tonnage of LME zinc stocks, one analyst said.

"Some of these large longs are indeed extremely substantial. Clearly that's going to show up in the large position data so if he's (King) looking for ammunition, he's got it. But what he does with it is anybody's guess," the analyst, who declined to be identified, said.
The nearby spreads for September will not come to the fore until after August delivery date next week, traders said.
"As we move towards those tight periods those longs are going to be really squeezing the shorts," one said.

"Once it gets past the August date, everything will focus on the September date and you will get the cash/day quoted. That would be the likely timing if there is going to be any action," the analyst said.
The LME may be under pressure to act from consumers and others forced to pay high premiums.
"The problem is the gentlemen hedgers are being squeezed in the middle, that business is being killed...It's extremely difficult to do physical business," a physical trader said.
Last week chief executive David King put out a notice, reminding market players not to abuse any dominant position in the market, but the following day zinc premiums ballooned.
"They're just laughing at the LME, it looks like a slap in the face," the physical trader said.
In the past, the LME has warned market players before taking action.
In June 1992, the last time the LME intervened in zinc, the premium of cash over three months peaked at $190 and the daily premium traded at $17.
The exchange published several warnings, then held an extraordinary board meeting, where it slapped a limit on the daily premium ranging from $15 to $5 depending on the dates.
The tightness was extreme in August 1989, when the premium to borrow metal for a day roared up to $90 per tonne and the cash over three months hit $230.
Tightness soon eased, however, and the exchange did not intervene until the end of the year when spreads flared again and the LME imposed a $20 limit on the daily premium.
--Eric Onstad, London Newsroom +44 171 542-8065
